passage:
Hey Afreen,
You asked what's new at school. Honestly, the best thing is our meme page. Me and Rustom made an account called "Pritam Daily" and we post edited pictures of him, his face on a crying baby, stuff like that. 200 followers already!
We also made a new chat for the class trip and just didn't add him. He'll figure it out.
It's weird. When I'm typing it, it feels like nothing. Just jokes on a screen. I never have to see his face when he reads them. Yesterday in the corridor he looked at me and I kind of looked away fast. Anyway.
How's college? Write back.
Zubin

qa.q: How many followers does the meme page have?
qa.a: It has 200 followers already.

qa.q: Why did Zubin look away fast in the corridor?
qa.a: Seeing Pritam's face in person made the jokes feel less like nothing, and Zubin probably felt a flicker of guilt.

qa.q: What could turn this around at this stage?
qa.a: Zubin could take the account down and add Pritam back, and Afreen could tell Zubin plainly that this is bullying and encourage a change to make it right.

qa.q: How does the meme page probably feel for Pritam?
qa.a: To Pritam it is heavy and public, with 200 people seeing edited pictures of him, while for Zubin it is only typing.

grounding: It shows mocking moving to edited photos, a fake account and exclusion from plans, feeling light to the sender behind a screen but heavy for the target.

passage:
Bidisha, you want to know about Tulika? Fine. I'm Nazia, and I'm not proud of this. Last year it started as jokes at lunch. Then it went online. Someone made a fake profile with her name and posted silly things as if she wrote them. We made a trip plan chat and just left her out. I sent the edited photo to three groups. I sent it from my bed, eating chips, laughing. It felt like nothing. Honestly, it felt like a game.
Then one day I passed her near the bus stop. She was holding her phone, and her eyes were swollen. She didn't even look angry, just empty. That's when it hit me. On my side it was one tap. On her side it was all day, every day.

qa.q: Where did Nazia pass Tulika?
qa.a: Nazia passed her near the bus stop.

qa.q: What did Nazia realise on seeing Tulika's face?
qa.a: Nazia realised that what felt light while lying in bed was heavy for Tulika all day, and Nazia seems to feel guilty.

qa.q: What could Nazia do now to start repairing the harm?
qa.a: Nazia could stop sharing, report the fake profile, apologise to Tulika and tell a trusted adult what happened so it can be dealt with.

qa.q: How might Bidisha react to hearing this?
qa.a: Bidisha might be shocked but also see that Nazia is being honest, and could encourage Nazia to act on that feeling.

grounding: It illustrates bullying escalating to a fake profile, edited photos and exclusion, with the screen making it feel light to the sender and heavy to the target.

passage:
Okay, I'll tell you how it went online. I'm Abhinav, and I was in the middle of it.

In class we'd just mimic Nitin's walk. Stupid, but face to face, you could see when he'd had enough, and you'd stop.

Then someone made a fake account with his photo, calling it "Nitin the Nerd." We'd post edited pictures: his face on a cartoon penguin, his head on a baby's body. I did some of the editing. It took two minutes. It felt like nothing. Just pixels.

We made a group for the class trip and didn't add him. He found out from the photos.

What I didn't see, behind my screen, was his face. I never saw him reading those posts at night. His cousin told me later he'd stopped eating dinner with his family.

That's the thing about screens. They made it light for me. It was never light for him.

qa.q: What was the fake account called?
qa.a: "Nitin the Nerd."

qa.q: How did the online cruelty feel to Abhinav at the time?
qa.a: It felt light, even amusing, to Abhinav, just pixels, because the screen hid Nitin's reactions; only later came guilt.

qa.q: What turning point could have stopped this, looking back?
qa.a: Refusing to edit the pictures or to leave Nitin out of the trip group, and reporting the fake account to a teacher or parent.

qa.q: How did the online bullying affect Nitin?
qa.a: It hit him much harder than Abhinav realised; he read the posts at night and stopped eating dinner with his family.

grounding: Abhinav describes mocking moving online through edited photos, a fake account and exclusion, where the screen made cruelty feel light to senders and heavy to Nitin.

passage:
Monday. In the corridor Varun and his friends had been calling Jagdish "Bhondu" for weeks. That evening Varun made a fake account with Jagdish's school photo and posted a video of a donkey with Jagdish's face on it. Forty likes by dinner. Varun laughed on his bed. It felt like a game.

Thursday, three days later. Varun made a group for Saturday's cricket and added everyone except Jagdish. Someone posted an edited photo of Jagdish crying. Varun added a laughing sticker without thinking.

Saturday. At the ground, Varun saw Jagdish watching from behind the fence, alone. Their eyes met for a second. Jagdish looked away. Varun felt something cold in his stomach. On his phone, the photos had seemed so light. Here, at the fence, Jagdish's face was heavy to look at.

qa.q: How many likes did the donkey video get by dinner?
qa.a: Forty.

qa.q: What did Varun feel when he met Jagdish's eyes at the fence?
qa.a: He felt a cold, uneasy guilt, as the real face made the cruelty feel heavy in a way the screen had not.

qa.q: What could Varun do after that moment at the fence?
qa.a: Delete the fake account and edited posts, apologise to Jagdish, and tell a teacher what happened so it can be fully stopped.

qa.q: What is it like for Jagdish to watch the match from behind the fence?
qa.a: He feels excluded and hurt, alone and aware that everyone else was invited.

grounding: Over a week Varun's mocking of Jagdish moves online through a fake account, edited photos and exclusion, feeling light on screen and heavy face to face.

passage:
Neelam, you asked why I got so angry when you laughed about that edited photo of your classmate. Let me, your Ujjwal mama, tell you something.

When I was in Class 10, around 2006, we'd just got our first social media accounts. There was a boy in our class, Sudhir. We started making fun of him on a forum: pasted his head onto a buffalo, made a fake profile of him writing silly poems.

On the screen it felt like nothing. A joke. I'd type something, laugh, close the computer and have dinner.

Then Sudhir stopped coming to school for two weeks. His mother came in. She had printed everything and laid it on the principal's desk.

That was the turning point. Seeing it on paper, on a desk, with his mother's hands shaking. What had felt light on the screen was very heavy for him.

qa.q: What did Sudhir's mother bring to the principal's desk?
qa.a: Printouts of everything that had been posted.

qa.q: How did the online mockery feel to Ujjwal at the time?
qa.a: It felt like nothing, just an amusing joke, easy to type and forget before dinner; the shame came only later.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ujjwal mama's story?
qa.a: When Sudhir's mother laid the printouts on the principal's desk, and Ujjwal saw how heavy it had been for Sudhir.

qa.q: How might Sudhir have felt during those two weeks away from school?
qa.a: He probably felt humiliated, isolated and afraid to face the class.

grounding: Ujjwal mama recalls online mocking through edited photos and a fake profile that felt light on screen but was heavy for the boy targeted.

passage: The monsoon had shut the school in Gangtok for three days, and Pema was bored. Stuck at home with patchy data and nothing but her phone, she opened the photo from the class trip: Avni mid-sneeze, eyes squeezed shut. A few taps and it had pig ears and a caption. She sent it to the girls' group. "STOP I can't breathe," someone replied. By the second rainy day Pema had set up a joke account in Avni's name, posting silly "thoughts", and the group was planning a sleepover for when school reopened, with everyone invited except Avni. From behind the screen it felt like a game, like doodling on a poster. Pema never saw Avni's face when the notifications arrived. She only saw the laughing replies, the rain on the window, and the follower count creeping up.

qa.q: Why was the school in Gangtok shut?
qa.a: The monsoon had shut the school for three days.

qa.q: Why did the cruelty feel so light to Pema?
qa.a: From behind the screen it felt like a harmless game; Pema was bored and pleased by the laughing replies, and never saw Avni's hurt.

qa.q: What could someone in the girls' group do at this stage?
qa.a: Someone could refuse to share the photo, report the fake account, tell a teacher or parent, and message Avni privately so she is not alone.

qa.q: What is Avni likely experiencing as the notifications arrive?
qa.a: Avni is probably humiliated and frightened, seeing her face mocked, her name used by a fake account and herself shut out of the sleepover.

grounding: Shows mockery escalating to an edited photo, a fake account and exclusion, with the screen making cruelty feel light to the sender.
